title: Banana Land Preparation: Clearing, Holing, Spacing and Drainage
metaTitle: Banana Land Preparation: Holes, Spacing, Drainage
metaDescription: Banana land preparation in the Philippines: plow and harrow, dig 40 to 50 cm holes, pick Lakatan or Cardava spacing and open drainage canals first.
excerpt: Good banana land preparation decides how well the mat stands, drains and fruits for years, because a banana is planted once and stays in the same spot. This guide walks through each step: clear the land, plow and harrow, lay out the rows, dig the holes and open drainage canals before any sucker goes in.

blocks.text: Spacing and hole sizes differ by variety and by farm, so use the numbers below as a starting point and ask your municipal agriculturist about your own soil.
Choose the site before you clear it

Banana needs moist, deep, fertile and well drained soil. It grows best in sandy loam or alluvial loam. It can stand a soil pH from 4.5 to 7.5, so test your soil first. Our guides for [acidic soil](/land-preparation/acidic-soil-preparation) and [sodic and alkaline soil](/land-preparation/sodic-alkaline-soil-preparation) cover what to do when the reading falls outside that range.

Flat land is the easiest to manage. Hilly or rolling land can also be used, but plan for erosion and adjust the planting distance and plant population.
Wind matters too. Banana plants are sensitive to strong winds, so farmers in windy places should provide windbreaks. In a typhoon belt, plan the windbreak rows now, because they take time to grow.
Banana land preparation step by step

items.title: Clear the land
items.text: Remove brush, old stumps and weeds. Manual clearing is best because banana fields are prepared with minimum soil disturbance. Never use a bulldozer, which damages the topsoil. Leave big stumps to decay and leave small branches to rot into organic matter. If the field grew bananas before, check for sick mats first. Fallow an infected area for 6 months to 1 year and burn infected plant parts using rice hull.

items.title: Plow and harrow thoroughly
items.text: Plow and harrow the field thoroughly to remove weeds and give the soil a good tilth. The right plowing depth depends on your soil, so follow what your local technician advises. A disc harrow helps where the topsoil is shallow, and compost can go in at that time.

items.title: Lay out the rows
items.text: Mark the rows with a measuring rope and stakes before you dig. Rows running east to west give every row an equal share of sunlight. On hills, lay the rows along the contour.

items.title: Dig the holes
items.text: Dig a hole at every stake, 40 cm wide and 40 cm deep. A larger hole of 50 cm on each side also works. Keep the topsoil apart.

items.title: Open the drainage canals
items.text: In flood prone areas, a good drainage system should be in place. In heavy rainfall areas, add trenches so water does not stand around the roots, which can rot them. Dig canals so water leaves the field.

blocks.text: Banana planting distance and field layout

Several things set the right banana planting distance: the variety, the slope and soil fertility. Sucker control and the use of machines also count. Close spaced plants must not touch their neighbors. These are the usual distances:

blocks.caption: Recommended banana planting distances
rows: Distance in the hill by between rows

blocks.text: Two layouts are common. In the square method, a plant sits at every corner of a square. In the quincunx system, one more plant sits at the center of each square. Topography, irrigation and equipment shape the layout. East to west rows give each row equal sunlight, and some farms run north to south rows for sunlight instead. So pick the direction that suits your slope, and ask your technician. On hillsides, plant along the contour to cut erosion.
Banana planting hole size and clean planting material

For the banana planting hole size, a hole of 40 cm by 40 cm is common. A larger hole of 50 cm by 50 cm by 50 cm is also used. So 40 to 50 cm on each side is a fair guide for the Philippines. The larger hole suits a tight or poor soil.

Dig the hole right after pegging. Put the topsoil in one pile and the rest of the soil in another. Set the plant upright, then fill the hole with topsoil first and the rest after, so the new roots grow in the most fertile soil. Compost or manure can also be worked into the soil during land preparation.

There are two kinds of planting material: tissue culture plantlets and sword leaf stage suckers. Select planting materials free from diseases. For Fusarium wilt, use tissue culture plants. Clean machines and tools that have been in a sick field as well. For nematodes, use nematode free suckers or tissue culture plants.

Suckers have a rule of their own. Pare the corm, plant within a week and do not keep suckers more than two weeks, because stored suckers yield less. Avoid planting where bananas grew before, unless the land rested for 2 to 3 years.

blocks.title: Planting sick material plants the disease
blocks.text: A banana mat that carries Fusarium wilt, Moko or bunchy top will infect the new field for years. Buy certified clean plantlets or suckers. Read about [banana bunchy top](/diseases/banana-bunchy-top) and [Moko disease](/diseases/moko-disease) before you buy.

Banana needs plenty of water. Yet it needs good drainage in flood prone areas. Drainage canals also help control banana freckles and Sigatoka, because standing water raises humidity and favors leaf disease. Good drainage helps control soil borne diseases too.

Dig the canals before planting, not after the first flood. Slope them so water runs out of the field. Read about [black Sigatoka](/diseases/black-sigatoka) to see what wet, humid fields invite.
Change the work by soil and season

items: Sandy loam and alluvial loam: the best soils for banana. Plow, harrow and plant.
Heavy clay that holds water: spend more effort on canals, because banana needs well drained soil.
Acidic soil: check the pH, because banana tolerates pH 4.5 to 7.5. Follow the [acidic soil guide](/land-preparation/acidic-soil-preparation) if you read below that.
Salty or sodic land: banana is not a salt tolerant crop, so read the [saline soil guide](/land-preparation/saline-soil-preparation) first.
Dry season: banana wants 20 to 22 cm of rain spread evenly each month, and growth suffers below 10 cm a month. Plan irrigation before you plant.
Wet season or typhoon areas: finish the canals and the windbreak first.
Planting suckers from a mat that looks tired or sick.
Digging holes but skipping the canals.
Planting too close, so leaves touch and humidity builds up.
Running the rows with no plan for the slope on a hillside.
Skipping the soil test, then finding out the pH is far from the range.

blocks.title: Put every land preparation day on the calendar
blocks.text: Add each lot to anee.io, set its planting date and the [cropping calendar](/features/cropping-calendar) dates the clearing, plowing, holing and canal digging back from planting. Hired hands and fertilizer go on the same board.
blocks.label: Start free

items.q: How big should the planting hole be for banana?
items.a: A hole 40 cm wide and 40 cm deep is common. A larger hole of 50 cm by 50 cm by 50 cm also works, with the topsoil kept separate. Ask your agriculturist if your soil is heavy or poor.

items.q: What is the planting distance for Lakatan?
items.a: The usual distance is 2.0 m in the hill by 2.5 m between rows, which gives 2,000 mats per hectare, or 3.0 m by 3.0 m for 1,111 mats per hectare.

items.q: Which direction should banana rows run?
items.a: East to west is common, so each row gets an equal share of sunlight. North to south rows are also used. On hillsides, plant along the contour.
Yes, in flood prone areas. Establish a good drainage system there. Drainage canals also help control freckles and Sigatoka.

items.q: Should I use suckers or tissue culture plants?
items.a: Both are used. Planting materials must be free from disease, and tissue culture plants keep Fusarium wilt out of clean farms.
